indiaMissions/india-company-charter-1813: Chaplains, the East India Company and the Charter Act of 1813
Calcutta (Kolkata)

Until 1813 the East India Company kept missionaries out of its territories, fearing that religious interference would provoke revolt. A group of evangelical Company chaplains — David Brown, Claudius Buchanan, Henry Martyn and Thomas Thomason — and their Clapham allies Charles Grant and William Wilberforce campaigned to change this. The Charter Act of 1813 allowed licensed missionaries into British India, created the bishopric of Calcutta and committed public money to education; the Act of 1833 removed the licence requirement.

The East India Company was a trading corporation that became a territorial power after Plassey (1757). Its directors believed that their rule depended on not offending Hindu and Muslim religious sensibilities, and they actively supported temples, festivals and pilgrimage sites through taxes and patronage. Missionaries without licences could be deported, as several Baptists and American Congregationalists discovered, and the Company's own Anglican chaplains were appointed to serve British soldiers and civilians, not to preach to Indians. Yet a small group of evangelical chaplains, many sponsored by Charles Simeon of Holy Trinity, Cambridge, used these posts to promote Christian teaching, translation and schools.

David Brown (1763–1812), who arrived in 1786, ran the Calcutta orphan school and the Old Church, and became provost of Fort William College. Claudius Buchanan (1766–1815), vice-provost of the college from 1800, sponsored oriental translations, published a Memoir on the Expediency of an Ecclesiastical Establishment for British India (1805), and in 1806–07 toured the south, visiting the St Thomas Christians of Travancore and the Jagannath festival at Puri. His Christian Researches in Asia (1811) painted Hindu practice in lurid terms and became a bestseller that fed public demand for missions. Henry Martyn (1781–1812), a Cornish senior wrangler and Simeon's protégé, served as chaplain at Dinapore (1806) and Cawnpore (1809), translating the New Testament into Hindustani (Urdu), revising Persian and Arabic versions, and gathering a few converts, notably the Muslim scholar Sheikh Salih, baptised as Abdul Masih in 1811. He left India in 1810 to perfect his Persian New Testament at Shiraz and died at Tokat in Anatolia in October 1812, aged 31; his journals made him a model of missionary self-sacrifice for generations.

In London, Charles Grant (1746–1823), a former Company servant converted in Bengal and later chairman of the Company's court of directors, wrote Observations on the State of Society among the Asiatic Subjects of Great Britain (1792), arguing that Britain had a duty to bring Christianity and Western knowledge to India. With William Wilberforce and the Clapham Sect he tried to insert 'pious clauses' into the Company's 1793 charter renewal, but the directors defeated them. The Vellore Mutiny of 1806, in which Indian sepoys killed British officers after dress regulations offended their religious customs, was blamed by some on missionary activity and strengthened the anti-missionary party, whose pamphleteers warned that preaching would cost Britain its empire.

The charter renewal of 1813 became a national campaign. Evangelical Anglicans, Baptists, Methodists and others organised hundreds of petitions to Parliament, and Wilberforce spoke at length in the Commons in June 1813, depicting Hindu society as cruel and degraded. The resulting Charter Act (53 Geo. III c. 155) allowed persons wishing to go to India 'for the purpose of introducing useful knowledge, and of religious and moral improvement' to apply for licences through the Board of Control, established a bishop of Calcutta with three archdeacons, and set aside not less than one lakh of rupees a year for the revival of literature and the promotion of science among Indians. The first bishop, Thomas Fanshaw Middleton, arrived in 1814 and founded Bishop's College, Calcutta (1820); his successor Reginald Heber (bishop 1823–26) toured north and south India and died at Trichinopoly in 1826.

The Act opened the way for the Church Missionary Society, the London Missionary Society, the Wesleyan Methodists, the American Board and others to work openly in British India, although licences could still be refused and Company officials remained cautious. The 1833 Charter Act abolished the licensing system, admitted missionaries of any nationality, and led to the creation of the dioceses of Madras (1835) and Bombay (1837). Evangelicals then turned to ending the Company's 'connection with idolatry' — its management of temple funds and pilgrim taxes at places such as Puri and Gaya — which was gradually dismantled from the late 1830s, the pilgrim tax being abolished in 1840. The debates of 1793–1833 fixed the terms of a lasting argument: whether British rule should be religiously neutral or actively Christian, and whether missions were allies or embarrassments of empire.

The chaplains' campaign transformed missions in India from a tolerated anomaly into a legally recognised enterprise and established the Anglican church in British India. It also created the enduring perception, exploited by critics then and now, that missions and empire went hand in hand — even though the Company remained wary of missionaries and many missionaries criticised colonial policy.

indiaMissions/india-duff-education/title: Alexander Duff and the English-education strategy in Bengal
indiaMissions/india-duff-education/summa: Alexander Duff, the Church of Scotland's first missionary to India, arrived in Calcutta in 1830 and opened a school that taught Western subjects and the Bible through English to upper-caste Hindu boys, hoping to undermine Hinduism intellectually and win the elite who would then influence the masses. His converts were few but prominent, his method was copied by Scottish and other missions across India, and he helped shape the colonial decision for English education and the founding of Indian universities.
indiaMissions/india-duff-education/story:
Alexander Duff (1806–1878) grew up at Moulin in Perthshire, studied at St Andrews under Thomas Chalmers, and in 1829 was appointed the first missionary of the Church of Scotland. His voyage was disastrous: the Lady Holland was wrecked near Cape Town in February 1830, and he lost his library, before a second near-wreck at the mouth of the Hooghly. Arriving in Calcutta in May 1830, he rejected the existing pattern of vernacular preaching to the poor. He argued instead that Hinduism was bound up with false science and history, which modern Western learning taught in English would dissolve; Christianity, taught alongside it, could fill the vacuum. Converts from the educated classes would then carry the faith 'downward' through Indian society.

On 13 July 1830 Duff opened the General Assembly's Institution on Chitpur Road, in a house provided with the help of the reformer Rammohun Roy, who supported English education though he did not accept orthodox Christianity. Pupils from Brahmin, Kayastha and other upper-caste families flocked to learn English, because English opened doors to government service and commerce. Duff taught a graded curriculum from the alphabet to university-level science, philosophy and political economy, with daily Bible instruction. He also delivered public lectures in 1830–31 aimed at the 'Young Bengal' students of Hindu College, disciples of Henry Derozio who had already abandoned orthodox Hinduism for rationalism.

The first conversions came from this circle. Mohesh Chunder Ghose and Krishna Mohan Banerjee (1813–1885), a Kulin Brahmin and Derozian editor, were baptised in 1832; Banerjee became an Anglican priest, a professor at Bishop's College and a noted Sanskrit scholar. Others followed — Gopinath Nundi, Anundo Chund Mazumdar, and later Lal Behari Day (1824–1892), who became a minister and the author of Bengal Peasant Life (1874). Each baptism provoked crisis: families mourned, pupils were withdrawn, and the Hindu press attacked the mission. Duff's converts were never more than a few dozen, but they formed an influential Bengali Christian intelligentsia.

Duff's influence on policy was considerable. He sided with the 'Anglicists' against the 'Orientalists' in the debate over whether government funds should support Sanskrit and Persian learning or English education; Thomas Babington Macaulay's Minute on Indian Education of February 1835 and Lord William Bentinck's resolution of March 1835 settled the matter in favour of English. Later Duff gave evidence before Parliament during the 1853 charter debates, helped shape Charles Wood's Education Despatch of 1854, which introduced grants-in-aid open to mission schools, and was among the founders of the University of Calcutta in 1857.

The Disruption of 1843 in the Church of Scotland split the mission: Duff and all his fellow missionaries joined the new Free Church, lost their buildings to the Established Church, and opened a new Free Church Institution in 1844. The two Scottish colleges were reunited in 1908 and later became the Scottish Church College, Calcutta. Duff's model spread rapidly: John Wilson founded what became Wilson College in Bombay, John Anderson opened the General Assembly's School in Madras in 1837 (later Madras Christian College), Stephen Hislop founded a school at Nagpur in 1844 (later Hislop College), and the CMS missionary Robert Noble opened a high school at Masulipatnam in 1843 (later Noble College). In Madras and Bombay, as in Calcutta, the baptism of a few high-caste students in 1839–43 caused mass withdrawals of pupils and public protests.

By the later nineteenth century the strategy had produced many colleges but few converts, and critics within the missions — including Rufus Anderson of the American Board and many evangelists — argued that education had become an end in itself. Supporters such as William Miller of Madras Christian College reframed it as 'preparation' that would Christianise Indian thought indirectly. The Christian colleges did educate many leaders of modern India, Hindu, Muslim and Christian alike, and contributed to the Bengal Renaissance and Indian nationalism, while the downward-filtration theory of conversion largely failed: Indian Christianity was to grow mainly through the mass movements of the poor rather than through the elite.
